chapters.title: What You Will Learn
verified_dimensions: Objectifs : le premier écran annonce trois acquis opérationnels correspondant à la leçon.
Organisation : cet écran ouvre la leçon avant les explications, la synthèse et l’évaluation prévue.
Média déclaré : la ressource possède un titre et une URL YouTube, interprétables par le lecteur historique.
Contextualisation visible contrôlée : aucun objectif avant lecture, question après visionnage, transcription ni alternative textuelle n’est renseigné dans ce bloc.
unverified_dimensions: Rendu navigateur réel, accessibilité multi-support, persistance de progression et comportement après authentification non testés en session applicative.
Disponibilité, contenu réel, exactitude pédagogique, sous-titrage et accessibilité de la vidéo YouTube non vérifiés ; l’URL renseignée n’est pas assimilée à une absence.

issues.description: La vidéo est présentée par son titre et son lecteur, sans objectif avant lecture, consigne d’observation, question post-visionnage, transcription ni alternative textuelle. LessonViewer rend ces éléments seulement lorsqu’ils sont renseignés ; il n’ajoute pas de contextualisation pédagogique par défaut. La cohérence fine avec le contenu externe n’est pas inférée du titre.
issues.current_content: title: 'vLLM: Easily Deploying & Serving LLMs'; url: 'https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q5IF2PHA5SA'. Champs objectiveBefore, questionsAfter, transcript et alternativeTextFr absents.
issues.proposed_content: Ajouter une introduction spécifique à la leçon « CPU, GPU, serverless and managed API tradeoffs » : objectif de visionnage, notion à repérer et utilisation dans la suite. Ajouter au minimum une question de réinvestissement ou une courte alternative textuelle/résumé ; si la ressource est générale ou longue, indiquer le segment utile. Valider ensuite cette contextualisation contre le contenu réel de la vidéo.

formation_summary.coverage: Revue qualitative exhaustive des 4 cours, 16 leçons, 96 chapitres, 16 activités checkpoint déclarées (48 questions) et 12 vidéos, à partir des JSON référencés par le manifest, du registre de blocs, de LessonViewer, chapterProgress, checkpointGate et YouTubePlayer.
key_findings: Les 16 checkpoints sont présents dans les JSON mais invisibles dans le parcours : tous sont dépourvus d’exerciseId, tous les catalogues exercises sont vides et aucun chapitre ne déclare type: checkpoint. Les évaluations ne sont donc ni affichées ni bloquantes.

Les 12 vidéos sont des ressources externes correctement référencées par URL/titre, mais aucune ne porte un objectif de visionnage, une question post-visionnage, une transcription ou une alternative textuelle dans les données. Elles ne sont pas déclarées absentes.
Une vidéo est placée après « Module Complete » dans chacun des quatre cours, sans optional: true ; elle conditionne la complétion de leçon sans activité d’exploitation associée.

Les 4 checkpoints du cours 02 contiennent en plus des choix génériques « Option A » à « Option D » : même après une réparation du rendu, ces choix ne permettraient pas à l’apprenant de raisonner sur les réponses.
positive_findings: La progression de chaque leçon est constante et intelligible dans les données : objectifs, concepts développés, synthèse, checkpoint, points clés, conclusion.
Les objectifs, développements, synthèses et messages de fin sont alignés sur les thèmes techniques annoncés ; aucun prérequis manifestement introduit après son usage n’a été confirmé.
Hors cours 02, les questions brutes des checkpoints sont généralement scénarisées, accompagnées de réponses discriminantes et d’explications ; leur défaut déterminant est leur non-rendu.
Le lecteur prévoit une stratégie de repli explicite si l’intégration YouTube échoue ; l’accessibilité et l’effectivité de ce repli n’ont pas été testées en navigateur.
formation_summary.score_interpretation: Les scores sont des appréciations qualitatives sur 100, renormalisées sur les dimensions inspectables au niveau de chaque chapitre. Les vidéos YouTube sont renseignées et rendables à partir de leur URL ; leur disponibilité, leur contenu réel, leur transcription effective, leur accessibilité et leur exactitude pédagogique n’ont pas été vérifiés. Elles ne sont jamais qualifiées d’absentes.
Aucune source externe n’a été utilisée ; la pertinence fine des vidéos n’est pas déduite de leur titre.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to choose between CPU, GPU, serverless, and managed APIs based on latency, throughput, and cost. 2) How workload shape (steady vs spiky) influences scaling strategies, batching, and cold starts. 3) How to estimate capacity and cost per request/token to select the right deployment model.

body.en: **Hardware choice: CPUs are general-purpose and cost-effective for small models, classical ML, and pre/post-processing; they struggle with large transformer inference due to limited parallelism. GPUs accelerate matrix ops and attention, delivering higher throughput per dollar for medium/large models (e.g., 7B+), especially with batching, quantization, and tensor cores. VRAM gates model size; quantization (INT8/4) and paged attention help fit models and increase throughput. Performance and cost: Latency targets (p50/p95), tokens/sec, and concurrency determine capacity. Batching trades single-request latency for throughput; dynamic batching and KV-cache reuse help. Aim for high utilization without breaching SLOs; estimate cost/request as (node_hourly_cost / sustained_req_per_hour). Hosting models: Self-managed (VMs/Kubernetes) offers full control, custom kernels, and predictable costs at the expense of operational overhead (autoscaling, observability, upgrades). Serverless functions are easy and scale-to-zero with per-invocation pricing but often CPU-only, have time/memory limits, and suffer cold starts. Serverless containers/Jobs add more resources and sometimes GPUs with autoscaling and simpler ops. Managed model APIs (e.g., vendor LLM endpoints) provide fastest time-to-value, strong SLAs, and enterprise features (security/compliance) but less control over models, limits on customization, data policies, and potentially higher variable cost. Workload shape: Steady traffic favors dedicated instances; spiky or sporadic workloads benefit from serverless or managed APIs with provisioned/warm capacity to mitigate cold starts. Data/compliance: Sensitive data may require VPC peering/private endpoints or self-hosting. Pricing gotchas: egress fees, per-token pricing variability, idle GPU burn, and spot/preemptible interruption rates.**

• Workload shape: Steady vs spiky demand dictates whether to use dedicated GPUs, serverless scale-to-zero, or managed APIs with warm pools.
• Throughput vs latency: Batching and quantization increase throughput/$ but can raise p95 latency—tune to SLOs and monitor utilization.
• Control vs convenience: Self-hosting maximizes control and predictability; serverless/managed minimize ops but limit customization and can increase variable cost.

• Match hardware and hosting model to workload shape, SLOs, and budget.
• Use batching, quantization, and utilization monitoring to optimize throughput/cost without violating latency SLOs.
• Prefer managed/serverless for bursty or low-ops needs; self-host for control, customization, and predictable steady loads.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the tradeoffs across CPU, GPU, serverless, and managed APIs and can choose the right approach for your AI workloads.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to build minimal, reproducible Docker images for CPU/GPU AI services. 2) How to package models and dependencies to reduce cold starts while keeping images maintainable. 3) How to run containers reliably with health checks, non-root users, and GPU configuration.

**Base images and compatibility: Choose a base aligned with your stack (e.g., python:3.11-slim for CPU, nvidia/cuda:<major.minor>-runtime for GPU). Ensure CUDA, cuDNN, and framework wheels (e.g., PyTorch/TensorFlow) match the host driver; runtime images are smaller than devel images. Build practices: Use multi-stage builds to compile artifacts then copy only runtime deps; pin versions with lockfiles; leverage .dockerignore; cache layers by installing dependencies before copying app code; clean APT caches and avoid unnecessary tools. Security and reproducibility: Run as a non-root user, minimize attack surface (slim images), scan images, and pin checksums for downloaded models. Packaging models: To reduce cold starts, either bake model weights into a separate image layer (updated occasionally) or implement a startup warm phase to download to a writable volume/cache; verify integrity via checksum. Serving: Provide an HTTP/gRPC interface (e.g., FastAPI + Uvicorn/Gunicorn) or a specialized server (Triton, vLLM, TGI). Configure ENTRYPOINT/CMD, HEALTHCHECK, and structured logging to stdout/stderr. Performance: Preload models on startup, enable torch.no_grad(), select dtype (e.g., float16/bfloat16), configure thread counts, and batch requests where appropriate. GPU runtime: Install NVIDIA Container Toolkit on hosts and run with --gpus; set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES as needed. Orchestration: Expose ports, add readiness/liveness/startup probes, and set resource limits/requests. For multi-arch (x86_64/arm64), use buildx and test images on target hardware.**

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design asynchronous inference using queues, workers, and result stores to avoid API timeouts 2) How to choose and configure messaging systems, delivery semantics, retries, and dead-letter queues 3) How to optimize throughput and latency with batching, backpressure, autoscaling, and idempotent processing

Asynchronous inference decouples request intake from model execution using a message queue and a worker pool. A typical flow: (1) The API receives a request, validates it, generates a job_id/idempotency key, stores large payloads in object storage if needed, and enqueues a small message (metadata + pointers). (2) The API immediately returns 202 Accepted with the job_id. (3) Workers pull messages, load the model (ideally pre-warmed), perform inference, and write results to a result store (cache/DB/object storage). (4) The client polls a GET /jobs/{id} endpoint, subscribes via WebSocket/SSE, or uses a callback/webhook to receive completion.

Select a queue based on semantics: RabbitMQ/SQS/Redis Streams for work queues; Kafka/PubSub for high-throughput streams and replays. Prefer at-least-once delivery with idempotent workers. Use visibility timeouts/acknowledgements, exponential backoff retries, and dead-letter queues (DLQs). Keep messages small; pass URIs to large inputs/outputs. Implement idempotency by upserting results keyed by job_id and ensuring side effects (writes, notifications) are safe to repeat.

Performance: Raise GPU/CPU utilization via micro-batching and dynamic batching (e.g., NVIDIA Triton), while bounding queueing delay (e.g., 10–50 ms). Group requests by shape (e.g., sequence length buckets) to reduce padding overhead. Apply backpressure using queue length limits, per-worker concurrency, and request shedding. Scale workers horizontally based on queue depth/lag, GPU utilization, and processing latency; isolate hot models with dedicated queues and autoscaling policies. Monitor throughput, p50–p99 latency, retries, DLQ size, and end-to-end SLA from request to result.

• Delivery semantics: at-least-once vs at-most-once, acknowledgements/visibility timeout, retry with exponential backoff, and dead-letter queues for poison messages
• Batching strategies: micro-batching/dynamic batching to raise GPU utilization while respecting latency budgets; bucketing/padding to align tensor shapes
• Backpressure and autoscaling: scale workers on queue depth/lag (e.g., with KEDA), cap concurrency, and shed load to protect latency SLOs

• Use a durable queue + worker pool to decouple intake from inference and avoid request timeouts
• Favor at-least-once delivery with idempotent workers, bounded retries, and DLQs; keep messages small and store large payloads externally
• Improve efficiency with dynamic batching, backpressure, and autoscaling on queue depth and GPU utilization
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to design and run asynchronous inference with queues, workers, batching, and robust delivery semantics.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to manage secrets securely (storage, injection, rotation, and access control) 2) How to structure configuration for services across dev/staging/prod using the 12‑factor approach 3) How to promote releases safely with GitOps/CI-CD, approvals, and progressive delivery

Secrets management: Store sensitive material (API keys, DB creds, tokens) in a dedicated secrets manager (e.g., cloud Secrets Manager, KMS-backed Kubernetes Secrets, or Vault). Encrypt at rest with KMS and in transit (TLS). Prefer workload identity (IAM roles/service accounts) to avoid long-lived static keys. Scope permissions via least privilege and namespacing. Rotate regularly with automation; use short-lived, dynamically issued credentials when available. Inject secrets at runtime via environment variables, mounted files/volumes, or a sidecar/agent; avoid baking into images or committing to Git. Audit access and changes.

Configuration management: Follow the 12-factor principle—config is externalized from the code. Use declarative manifests and templates (Helm/Kustomize/Terraform) with environment overlays to vary endpoints, feature flags, and resource limits. Validate config with schemas and enforce policies (OPA/Conftest). Keep a clear precedence order and default-safe values.

Environment promotion: Build once, promote the same artifact (image digest) from dev → staging → prod. Use GitOps: desired state (manifests/overlays) lives in Git; promotions are PRs that change only environment references (e.g., image tag/digest or Helm values). A controller (e.g., Argo CD/Flux) reconciles after approvals and automated checks (tests, security/policy scans). Apply progressive delivery (canary/blue‑green) with health gates (SLOs, error budget, latency, rollback on regression). Ensure database migrations are safe (backward compatible/online). Maintain audit trails and drift detection.

• Secret management best practices: encryption with KMS, least privilege IAM, rotation/dynamic creds, and runtime injection (not in images/Git)
• Build once, promote via GitOps using immutable image digests and environment overlays for config differences
• Progressive delivery: canary/blue‑green with automated health checks, approval gates, and fast rollback

• Centralize secrets with KMS-backed storage, least-privilege access, and automated rotation; inject at runtime, never in images or Git
• Externalize and template configuration; build once and promote the same artifact via GitOps with environment overlays
• Use progressive delivery with health gates and rollbacks to safely promote changes across environments
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now manage secrets and configuration securely and promote releases safely across environments.

body.en:
In this lesson you will learn:

- 1) How core Kubernetes primitives (Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps/Secrets, Volumes) map to AI inference and batch workloads
- 2) How to configure probes, resources, autoscaling, and rollouts for resilient model serving
- 3) How to assemble a minimal, secure, observable model-serving stack using native K8s or operators like KServe

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
Pods are the atomic unit of scheduling and run one or more containers that share networking and volumes. For AI inference, a Pod typically runs a model server (e.g., NVIDIA Triton, TorchServe, or a FastAPI/Uvicorn app) plus optional sidecars for logging, metrics, or model downloaders. Deployments manage stateless replicas and enable rolling updates, canaries, and self-healing via ReplicaSets. Use StatefulSets when stable network IDs and persistent storage are required (e.g., sharded vector indexes or on-disk caches). Jobs and CronJobs run finite tasks such as offline batch scoring, data preparation, or model evaluation.

Services provide a stable virtual IP/DNS name for Pods; use ClusterIP internally, NodePort/LoadBalancer for external access, and Ingress or a Gateway (or a service mesh) to handle HTTP routing, TLS, and traffic policies. ConfigMaps and Secrets decouple configuration from images—store model URIs, feature flags, and API tokens; mount them as env vars or volumes. Volumes and PersistentVolumeClaims (via CSI drivers) hold model weights, embeddings, and caches; emptyDir or ephemeral-storage limits support scratch space. Use readiness probes to gate traffic until a model is warmed, liveness probes to recover from deadlocks, and startup probes for long cold starts. Resource requests/limits guide scheduling and protect nodes; pair them with Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) on CPU, memory, or custom metrics (e.g., queue depth via KEDA) to meet latency SLOs.

Adopt Pod Disruption Budgets to preserve capacity during maintenance, and topology constraints or anti-affinity to spread replicas. Employ RBAC, Namespaces, and NetworkPolicies for least-privilege and isolation. Run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem when possible; mount only the volumes you need. Expose Prometheus metrics and structured logs for observability; use tracing to follow request flows. Operators/CRDs such as KServe provide higher-level abstractions (e.g., canary routing, dynamic scaling, model management) atop these primitives.

• Pod: Smallest deployable unit; one or more containers sharing network and volumes
• Deployment/ReplicaSet: Manages stateless replicas, rollouts, rollbacks, and self-healing
• Service/Ingress: Stable service discovery and external HTTP(S) routing to your model endpoints
• ConfigMap/Secret: Externalize configuration and credentials; mount as env vars or files
• Volumes/PVC/CSI: Persistent and ephemeral storage for model weights, caches, and artifacts
• Probes/HPA: Readiness/liveness/startup probes for resilience; autoscale on CPU/custom metrics
• Jobs/CronJobs: Finite, batch-style AI tasks such as offline inference or preprocessing
• Operators/CRDs (e.g., KServe): Higher-level model-serving APIs and traffic management

• Deployments + Services + HPA are the backbone of scalable, reliable inference endpoints
• Probes, resource requests/limits, and PDBs improve correctness, availability, and operability
• ConfigMaps/Secrets and PVCs cleanly separate configuration, credentials, and model artifacts

Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how core Kubernetes primitives map to AI inference and batch workloads, and can apply them to build secure, observable, and scalable services.

title.en: GPU scheduling, node pools, taints and tolerations

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How GPUs are exposed to Kubernetes via the NVIDIA device plugin and GPU Operator 2) How to schedule GPU workloads using extended resources, node pools, labels, taints/tolerations, and affinity 3) Techniques for multi-GPU, MIG, time-slicing, and autoscaling dedicated GPU capacity

GPUs are advertised to Kubernetes through a device plugin (commonly NVIDIA's). Workloads request GPUs as extended resources (e.g., resources.requests/limits: {"nvidia.com/gpu": 1}). Best practice is to set equal requests and limits for GPUs; native overcommit is not supported. The device plugin injects environment variables (e.g., CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) and mounts to make allocated devices available within containers.

Use dedicated GPU node pools (separate node groups) with labels (e.g., accelerator=nvidia) to target placement and simplify autoscaling. Taint GPU nodes (e.g., nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule) so only Pods with matching tolerations can land there, preventing accidental scheduling of CPU-only workloads. Combine nodeSelector or node/pod affinity with tolerations to precisely control placement. For spreading or bin-packing, use topologySpreadConstraints, anti-affinity, and PriorityClasses to protect latency-critical inference from preemption.

Multi-GPU Pods request multiple devices on a single node (e.g., "nvidia.com/gpu": 4). For A100/H100, Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions a physical GPU into isolated profiles (e.g., 1g.5gb). With the NVIDIA GPU Operator and MIG enabled, the device plugin advertises profile-specific resources (e.g., nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb), allowing fine-grained scheduling. Time-slicing (via device plugin configuration) and NVIDIA MPS can increase utilization for small inference workloads, at the cost of strict isolation compared to MIG.

Topology awareness matters for performance. Kubernetes' topology manager can align CPU, memory, and PCIe devices (e.g., single-numa-node policy), reducing cross-NUMA traffic. NVIDIA GPU Feature Discovery labels nodes with GPU capabilities to aid scheduling decisions. For runtime, use a RuntimeClass configured with nvidia-container-runtime when required by your environment. Operationally, the NVIDIA GPU Operator automates driver, toolkit, DCGM exporter, and device plugin deployment.

Autoscaling GPU capacity typically uses a separate autoscaling node group for GPU instances. The HPA (or KEDA for custom metrics like queue length) scales Pods; the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter then adds/removes GPU nodes to satisfy unschedulable Pods. Monitor GPU utilization and memory with DCGM/Prometheus and set PriorityClasses so critical inference preempts lower-priority batch jobs if necessary.

body.en:
• NVIDIA device plugin: Exposes GPUs as extended resources to the scheduler
• Extended resources: Request GPUs with "nvidia.com/gpu"; set requests=limits for correct allocation
• Dedicated GPU node pools: Separate node groups with labels for targeting and cost control
• Taints/tolerations: Isolate GPU nodes (e.g., nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule) to admit only GPU Pods
• Affinity/anti-affinity & topology spread: Control placement, spread load, and avoid noisy neighbors
• MIG and time-slicing: Partition GPUs or share via slices; trade isolation vs. utilization
• PriorityClasses/preemption: Protect latency-critical inference from being evicted by lower-priority work
• Autoscaling: HPA/KEDA scales Pods; Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter scales GPU nodes

• Request GPUs via extended resources and isolate capacity with taints/tolerations and labels
• Use MIG for strong isolation or time-slicing for higher utilization of small workloads
• Scale Pods with HPA/KEDA and scale GPU nodes with Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter

Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now schedule GPU workloads effectively using node pools, taints/tolerations, affinity, and autoscaling, and choose between MIG or time-slicing for utilization and isolation.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) What the NVIDIA GPU Operator is and the components it manages in Kubernetes 2) How to install and configure the operator (drivers, device plugin, DCGM, NFD, MIG) across different environments 3) Operational best practices for upgrades, security, scheduling, and troubleshooting

The NVIDIA GPU Operator automates deployment and lifecycle management of NVIDIA GPU software on Kubernetes clusters. It installs and reconciles GPU stack components as DaemonSets/Deployments and CRs so nodes become GPU-ready without manual steps.

Key components managed:
• NVIDIA Driver: Provides kernel modules and user-space libraries. The operator can deploy a driver container (privileged) or be configured to use pre-installed/cloud-managed drivers (driver.enabled=false).
• NVIDIA Container Toolkit: Enables Docker/Containerd runtimes to expose GPUs inside containers (nvidia-container-runtime, libnvidia-container).
• Kubernetes Device Plugin: Discovers GPUs and advertises the extended resource nvidia.com/gpu. It performs health checks and can support time-slicing and MIG-aware scheduling.
• DCGM + DCGM Exporter: Data Center GPU Manager provides low-level telemetry and health; the exporter exposes Prometheus metrics for observability.
• MIG Manager (on MIG-capable GPUs such as A100/H100): Automates creation of MIG profiles/instances according to a ClusterPolicy, enabling GPU partitioning.
• Node Feature Discovery (optional): Labels nodes with GPU capabilities (e.g., vendor, model, MIG profiles) to enable topology-aware scheduling via nodeSelectors/affinity.
• NVIDIA Fabric Manager (NVSwitch/NVLink systems): Manages fabrics on multi-GPU servers for high-bandwidth interconnects.

Installation patterns:
• Helm chart or OperatorHub/OLM: Apply a ClusterPolicy to toggle components (drivers, toolkit, dcgm, mig, nfd) and set version pinning.
• OpenShift: The operator can leverage the Driver Toolkit to build driver modules matching the cluster kernel.
• Managed clouds (GKE/AKS/EKS): Often drivers are provided by the platform; deploy the operator with driver disabled but keep device plugin, toolkit, and DCGM for standardized scheduling/telemetry.

Scheduling and isolation:
• Request GPUs with resource requests/limits on nvidia.com/gpu. One integer unit maps to one full GPU unless using MIG or time-slicing.
• MIG partitions a GPU into isolated GPU Instances/Compute Instances; the device plugin advertises granular resources (e.g., nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb).
• Time-slicing (via device plugin configs) multiplexes a GPU among pods with enforced timeslices; less isolation than MIG but higher utilization.

Operations and security:
• Privileged DaemonSets are required for driver/toolkit components; restrict node selection and apply PodSecurity/NetworkPolicies.
• Upgrades are coordinated by the operator; drain nodes where necessary to reload drivers or reconfigure MIG.
• Troubleshooting uses operator and component logs, device plugin health endpoints, and DCGM metrics to trace issues.

• ClusterPolicy CR: Central configuration object controlling which GPU components the operator installs and how they are versioned and configured
• Device Plugin Resources: GPUs are advertised as nvidia.com/gpu (or MIG-specific resources) and consumed via pod resource requests/limits for scheduling
• MIG vs Time-Slicing: MIG provides hard isolation and QoS guarantees; time-slicing shares a GPU without memory isolation, trading determinism for utilization

• The GPU Operator automates end-to-end GPU stack management (drivers, toolkit, device plugin, DCGM, MIG)
• Use ClusterPolicy to enable/disable components and align with your environment (on-prem vs managed cloud)
• Choose MIG for strong isolation or time-slicing for higher sharing; schedule via nvidia.com/* resources and node labels

Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how the NVIDIA GPU Operator equips Kubernetes clusters for GPU workloads and how to configure it for isolation, telemetry, and reliable scheduling.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to collect GPU telemetry in Kubernetes using DCGM, Prometheus, and Grafana 2) Which GPU health and performance metrics matter and how to alert on them 3) Common GPU failure modes (OOM, throttling, ECC, Xid errors, device health) and remediation strategies

Telemetry pipeline:
• DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) exposes low-level stats (utilization, memory, power, clocks, temperature, ECC, NVLink/PCIe). The dcgm-exporter (usually deployed by the GPU Operator) publishes Prometheus metrics per GPU/MIG instance.
• Prometheus scrapes dcgm-exporter and stores time series; Grafana dashboards visualize GPU utilization, memory headroom, ECC, thermals, and per-pod usage (via labels).
• Complementary tools: nvidia-smi for ad-hoc inspection; dcgmi for health checks; node logs (dmesg, driver logs) for Xid codes.

Key metrics to monitor and alert on:
• Utilization and saturation: sm_util, mem_copy_util, and memory_used vs memory_total for headroom and capacity planning.
• Thermal/power: temperature, power_draw vs power_limit; throttle_reasons indicating thermal or power capping.
• Reliability: correctable/uncorrectable ECC errors; Xid error counts; PCIe replay errors; NVLink link states.
• Health and availability: device plugin health status; time to first byte/latency at the application layer to catch soft failures.
• MIG awareness: metrics per MIG device (e.g., memory usage of a 1g.5gb slice) to avoid overcommit.

Common failure modes and remediation:
• GPU OOM (CUDA out-of-memory): Application allocates more device memory than available (or than a MIG slice provides). Remediate by reducing batch size, enabling gradient checkpointing, using memory-efficient kernels, or requesting larger/MIG-suitable resources.
• Throttling (thermal/power): High temperatures or power limits cause clocks to drop. Improve chassis airflow, clean filters, raise power limits within spec, or lower workload intensity; monitor throttle_reasons to distinguish thermal vs power cap.
• ECC errors: Spikes in correctable errors may precede uncorrectable faults; persistent uncorrectable ECC may require node drain, GPU reset, or RMA. Enable alerts and track trend lines.
• Xid errors: Driver-reported faults like memory page faults or device loss; e.g., Xid 31 (GPU memory page fault), Xid 79 (GPU has fallen off the bus). Often results in CUDA context loss and pod restarts. Investigate PCIe stability, drivers, and thermals; consider firmware/driver updates.
• Device plugin health failures: The plugin marks devices unhealthy; scheduler avoids them. Drain the node, inspect driver/DCGM logs, and perform a GPU reset or node reboot.
• MIG reconfiguration issues: Changing MIG mode or profiles requires GPUs to be idle; operator may drain pods before reconfiguring. Ensure proper disruption windows and PDBs.
• Infrastructure-induced failures: Insufficient PSU, overheating, or flaky risers/NVLink bridges can manifest as intermittent Xids and performance drops; validate hardware health.

Alerting and SLOs:
• Define alerts for high memory utilization, sustained thermal throttling, rising ECC, and recurrent Xids per device.
• Create availability SLOs that combine GPU readiness (device healthy), pod success rate, and latency tail metrics to capture user impact.
• Runbooks should include quick commands (nvidia-smi, dcgmi diag), log paths, and remediation steps (cordon/drain, reset, rollback drivers).

• DCGM Exporter: Exposes standardized GPU metrics for Prometheus, including MIG-aware labels for per-slice visibility
• Xid Errors: Driver-level error codes indicating GPU faults; repeated or severe Xids often require node drain, driver/firmware updates, or hardware checks
• GPU OOM vs Pod OOM: CUDA OOM occurs on device memory and restarts the app; Pod OOMKill is from system memory pressure—telemetry distinguishes these paths

• Use DCGM + Prometheus to monitor utilization, memory, thermals, power, ECC, and Xid errors (including per-MIG visibility)
• Most production issues trace to memory exhaustion, throttling, or hardware/driver faults—alert early and follow runbooks
• Isolate unhealthy devices via the device plugin and Kubernetes drain workflows to protect SLOs while you remediate
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now implement GPU telemetry pipelines, interpret health signals, and respond effectively to common failure modes.

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
Serving patterns: Online (sync) inference optimizes tail latency for interactive workloads, often with streaming tokens; Async/batch optimizes throughput and cost for non-interactive jobs by queueing requests. Single-tenant vs multi-tenant: Dedicated-model pods simplify isolation; multi-model servers improve GPU utilization by loading/evicting models on demand with a loading cache.

Stateless vs stateful: Keep application servers stateless and manage state (tokens, KV cache) in the inference tier; persistent KV cache can reduce time-to-first-token (TTFT) for continued chats. Throughput tactics: Micro/continuous batching merges requests at decode time for higher tokens/sec without large latency penalties; request admission and max queue times protect SLOs.

Parallelism: Tensor parallelism (TP) shards model weights across GPUs; pipeline parallelism (PP) splits layers into stages—choose the smallest configuration that meets latency targets to limit cross-GPU overhead. Caching and quantization: Tokenization cache, prompt cache, and KV cache reuse speed up repeated prompts; quantization (e.g., 8/4-bit) reduces memory footprint with some quality/speed trade-offs.

Platform: Containerize the inference server behind an API gateway and a request router; use K8s with HPA/KEDA to scale on GPU utilization, queue depth, or tokens/sec. Operations: Rate limiting and per-tenant quotas prevent overload; blue/green or canary rollouts limit risk; observability should track TTFT, decode tokens/sec, queue latency, cache hit rate, error codes, and cost per 1k tokens.

• Online vs async/batch: Optimize for p95 latency vs throughput/cost by choosing synchronous or queued processing.
• Single- vs multi-model serving: Dedicated pods simplify isolation; multi-tenant servers maximize GPU utilization via on-demand loading/eviction.
• Batching, caching, and parallelism: Continuous batching + KV/prompt caching + right-sized TP/PP deliver strong tokens/sec with acceptable latency.

• Choose online vs async/batch based on interactivity, SLOs, and cost.

title.en: Batching, KV cache, throughput and latency optimization

body.en:
In this lesson you will learn:

- 1) How vLLM’s continuous batching and scheduling work and how to tune them for different traffic patterns. 2) How the KV cache and PagedAttention manage memory and speed, including prompt/prefix caching and prefill vs. decode behavior. 3) Practical techniques to optimize throughput and latency: controlling concurrent sequences and batched tokens, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, and sizing to GPU memory limits.

LLM serving has two phases: prefill (encoding the entire prompt) and decode (generating tokens iteratively). Prefill is compute- and memory-heavy at sequence length, while decode is dominated by many small steps. vLLM increases efficiency with continuous batching: it admits new requests and merges them dynamically, interleaving decode steps across many sequences so the GPU stays busy. This improves tokens-per-second (TPS) without waiting for batch boundaries.

KV cache stores the key/value tensors for each layer and token so the model can reuse past context during decoding. vLLM implements PagedAttention, which organizes KV tensors into fixed-size blocks that can be allocated, reused, and evicted without large contiguous allocations. This reduces fragmentation and allows high GPU memory utilization while supporting many concurrent sequences. Prompt/prefix caching lets requests that share the same prefix (e.g., a common system prompt) reuse precomputed KV blocks, dramatically reducing prefill time.

Throughput–latency trade-offs: increasing the number of concurrent sequences or the total tokens processed per step raises throughput but can increase per-request and tail latency (head-of-line blocking), especially when long prompts arrive. Techniques to mitigate this include limiting the maximum number of batched tokens, capping concurrent sequences, and using chunked prefill so long prompts are processed in smaller slices that interleave fairly with decoding traffic. Speculative decoding (using a cheap draft model or lookahead) can boost decode TPS when acceptance rates are high. Hardware parallelism (e.g., tensor parallelism across GPUs) increases capacity but introduces inter-GPU communication; choose sizes that match your interconnect bandwidth. Always budget KV cache memory for worst-case context and output lengths; longer contexts linearly increase KV memory usage and can reduce the number of sequences that fit concurrently.

• Continuous batching: Dynamically merges and schedules requests so decode steps from many sequences share GPU time, maximizing utilization.
• KV cache with PagedAttention: Stores past keys/values in fixed-size blocks to reduce fragmentation, enable reuse/eviction, and support prompt/prefix caching.
• Throughput–latency knobs: Limit concurrent sequences and batched tokens, use chunked prefill for long prompts, consider speculative decoding, and size context/output to fit GPU memory.

• Continuous batching and chunked prefill help balance throughput and tail latency under mixed traffic.
• PagedAttention-backed KV cache and prefix caching are central to vLLM’s efficiency and memory scalability.
• Tune concurrency (sequences and batched tokens) and context/output limits to meet TPS targets within GPU memory and latency SLOs; consider speculative decoding for additional decode speedups.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how vLLM batches requests, manages the KV cache, and how to optimize throughput and latency in practice.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to assemble a production-grade vLLM serving stack: networking, storage, observability, and CI/CD.
- 2) Request routing patterns for multi-model, multi-replica clusters, including session affinity and canarying.
- 3) Autoscaling strategies using queue depth, tokens/sec, and GPU metrics to meet latency SLOs while controlling cost.

A typical production architecture includes: an API gateway (auth, rate limiting, TLS), a request router, a pool of vLLM servers (each managing one or more GPUs), model storage (e.g., object storage for weights), feature/config management, and observability (metrics, logs, traces). For Kubernetes, use a Service/Ingress in front of vLLM pods; in VM environments, place a load balancer in front of instances.

Routing: Keep request affinity for the lifetime of a generation to preserve KV cache in the chosen replica. Route by model ID and replica health; use weighted routing for canary releases and gradual traffic shifting between model versions. For multi-GPU tensor-parallel models, treat each replica as a placement group and avoid mid-request re-routing. Employ priority queues or per-tenant limits to protect SLOs and fairness.

Observability and SLOs: Track queue time, time-to-first-token (TTFT), tokens/sec (prefill and decode), P50/P95/P99 latency, GPU utilization and memory, KV block usage, and error rates (OOM, timeout, overload). Export metrics to Prometheus and visualize with Grafana; use logs for prompts/latency (with privacy controls) and traces to see where time is spent.

Autoscaling: Scale replicas based on leading indicators (request queue depth or admitted-but-waiting tokens) rather than only GPU utilization. Tokens-per-second per replica is a capacity metric; when observed load approaches capacity and queue time rises, scale out. For Kubernetes, combine Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) or KEDA with custom metrics (e.g., queued requests, queued tokens, TTFT). Pair with a Cluster Autoscaler to add GPU nodes. Consider scale-to-zero for low-traffic models with warm pools to reduce cold-start impact. Right-size pods to GPU memory and enable GPU partitioning (MIG) when appropriate to run multiple small models per GPU without interference.

Resilience: Use readiness/liveness probes, surge/rolling upgrades, and canaries to limit blast radius. Keep model weights in local persistent cache to reduce cold-load times; pre-warm frequently used models. Implement backpressure: when queues exceed thresholds, shed load gracefully or return retry-after to keep SLOs.

• Session affinity: Keep a request stream on the same replica to reuse KV cache and avoid restarts mid-generation.
• SLO-driven routing and scaling: Use queue time, TTFT, and tokens/sec as primary signals; apply weighted routing for canaries and A/B tests.
• Kubernetes/VM integration: Pair vLLM replicas with autoscaling (HPA/KEDA + cluster autoscaler), GPU-aware scheduling, and comprehensive observability to manage cost and reliability.

• Production readiness hinges on session-aware routing, robust observability, and controlled rollouts.
• Autoscale on leading indicators like queue depth and tokens/sec, and pair pod autoscaling with GPU node autoscaling.
• Keep models warm, use canaries and weighted routing for safe changes, and implement backpressure to protect latency SLOs under load.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design a production stack for vLLM, route traffic intelligently, and autoscale to meet SLOs reliably.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design effective liveness, readiness, and startup health checks for ML model servers 2) How to plan and execute realistic load, stress, spike, and soak tests to validate SLOs 3) How to interpret latency percentiles, error rates, and saturation signals to set safe capacity and avoid false positives.

body.en:
Health checks ensure a service is running and ready to receive traffic.

Liveness probes answer whether the process should be restarted; keep them simple and fast (e.g., thread/event loop alive).

Readiness probes verify dependencies needed to serve requests, such as the model loaded in memory, GPU availability, tokenizer present, or connection to feature stores; fail readiness to remove the pod from load balancing without restarts.

Startup probes prevent premature liveness failures during cold start and model warm-up.

In Kubernetes, configure probe endpoints with sensible timeouts, periods, and failure thresholds to avoid flapping.

For gRPC, use the standard gRPC health checking protocol; for HTTP, expose lightweight /live, /ready endpoints.

Load testing validates that the service meets SLOs (e.g., p95 and p99 latency, error rate) at target QPS/RPS and concurrency.

Use realistic request distributions (payload sizes, token lengths) and warm up models to avoid cold-start bias.

Prefer open-loop traffic (rate-based) to evaluate queueing behavior and tail latency; closed-loop (concurrency-based) is useful for client perspective.

Examine resource telemetry (CPU, GPU utilization, memory, I/O, network) and saturation indicators (queue depth, in-flight requests).

Tools include k6, Locust, JMeter, Vegeta, wrk2; coordinate distributed generators and isolate the system under test.

Identify capacity inflection points and implement backpressure, timeouts, and autoscaling policies.

• Liveness vs Readiness vs Startup: Liveness checks process health; readiness checks serving capability and dependencies; startup gates initial warm-up.
• Open-loop vs Closed-loop testing: Rate-based traffic reveals queueing and tail latency; concurrency-based tests reflect client throughput under backpressure.
• Tail latency and SLOs: Track p95/p99 latency and error rates; manage with request limiting, batching, autoscaling, and resource isolation.

• Keep liveness simple; put dependency checks in readiness; use startup to cover cold-start and model warm-up.
• Validate SLOs with realistic, rate-based load tests, watching tail latency, error budgets, and resource saturation.
• Control tail latency with backpressure, batching, and autoscaling; set probe thresholds and timeouts to avoid flapping.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to design robust health checks and execute meaningful load tests to ensure reliable model serving.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How blue/green and canary releases reduce risk and downtime 2) How to define metrics, guardrails, and automated rollback policies 3) How to manage schema, config, and model version compatibility for safe rollbacks.

Blue/green keeps two production-ready environments: blue (current) and green (new).

You validate green, warm caches and models, then switch traffic via load balancer, Ingress, or service mesh for near-zero downtime and instant rollback.

Canary gradually shifts a small percentage of live traffic to the new version while monitoring guardrails such as error rate, p95/p99 latency, cost per request, and business KPIs; traffic increases only if metrics remain within thresholds.

Automated rollback reverts to the last good artifact or configuration when guardrails are breached for a sustained window.

Kubernetes supports rolling updates, and tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger automate blue/green and canary with Prometheus-based analysis; service meshes (e.g., Istio/Linkerd) handle weighted routing.

Safe rollbacks require backward-compatible APIs and database schemas (expand/contract migrations), immutable builds, and versioned models/tokenizers.

ML-specific considerations include validating model outputs offline before exposure, shadow traffic to compare responses, segment-based canaries (by user cohort or request features), and ensuring tokenizer/vocabulary and preprocessing pipelines are compatible across versions.

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to design multi-provider/model fallback using health checks, timeouts, circuit breakers, and routing policies.
- 2) How to implement graceful degradation patterns (reduced features, cached or summarised results, smaller/local models) to protect user experience under failures or quota limits.
- 3) How to measure, test, and monitor fallback effectiveness with SLIs/SLOs, retry budgets, tracing, and chaos testing while maintaining security and compliance.

Provider fallback ensures continuity when a primary LLM/model or vendor is slow, unavailable, rate-limited, or returns errors.

Common failure modes include latency spikes (tail latency), HTTP/transport failures, quota exhaustion (429), token/context limit errors, and regional outages.

Robust clients use layered defenses: timeouts aligned to user SLAs, bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers to stop calling unhealthy dependencies.

Hedged requests can reduce tail latency by racing a secondary provider and canceling the loser.

Fallback policies should be explicit decision trees (e.g., primary -> secondary -> local model -> cached template) guided by health signals, cost ceilings, and compliance rules (data residency, PII handling).

Graceful degradation prioritizes delivering a useful, cheaper result over failing hard: shorten context, switch to a smaller or distilled model, return a cached/previous answer, or provide a structured error with next steps.

Observability is essential: track SLIs such as success rate, p95 latency, fallback rate, and user-visible quality metrics; use tracing to attribute time spent per provider and to confirm cancellations work.

Test the plan with fault injection (timeouts, 429s), chaos experiments, and game days.

Document runbooks for when to change weights, disable a provider, or adjust budgets.

• Circuit breaker: Stops calls to an unhealthy provider after error/latency thresholds, then probes (half-open) before resuming.
• Hedged requests: Send a duplicate request to an alternate provider after a short delay; use the first successful response and cancel the rest to cut tail latency at some extra cost.
• Graceful degradation: Predefined fallback behaviors (reduced context, simpler prompts, cached/approximate answers, local model inference) that preserve core functionality under stress while meeting SLOs and compliance constraints.

• Design explicit fallback decision trees guided by health signals, cost, and compliance.
• Use bounded timeouts, backoff, circuit breakers, and (optionally) hedged requests to control tail latency and errors.
• Measure and test with SLIs/SLOs, tracing, and chaos experiments; document runbooks and guardrails for safe operation.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to design provider fallback and graceful degradation strategies, instrument them, and operate them safely in production.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to run a production readiness review (PRR) for AI model serving, including SLOs, capacity, security, and resilience.
- 2) How to plan safe releases using canary/blue–green, feature flags, and automated rollback with runbooks and on-call readiness.
- 3) How to validate readiness with load/soak tests, quality evaluations, monitoring/alerting, cost guardrails, and disaster recovery objectives.

A production readiness review (PRR) is a cross-functional checklist and sign-off that confirms a system can meet user and business requirements under real traffic.

Define SLIs (e.g., success rate, p95 latency, quality/hallucination rate, cost per request) and SLOs with error budgets to gate releases.

Validate capacity with load tests (peak + margin), stress/failover tests, and soak tests to uncover leaks.

Ensure environment parity and automated, reproducible deployments.

Choose a release strategy: canary (progressive traffic shifting based on guardrail metrics), blue–green (switch between two identical environments), or feature flags (enable/disable behavior without redeploying).

Prepare operational readiness: dashboards, actionable alerts (symptom-based), logging/tracing, runbooks, and on-call rotations.

Establish rollback that is fast and safe (one-click, versioned artifacts, backward-compatible schemas/prompts).

Address security and privacy: mTLS, authZ, secrets management, PII redaction, data residency, vendor risk.

Plan disaster recovery with RTO/RPO and test backups and regional failover.

For AI systems, integrate offline/online evaluation, canary quality gates, prompt/model versioning, and dataset lineage.

Add cost controls (quotas, budgets, rate limiting) to prevent runaway spend.

• SLOs and error budgets: Quantified targets (e.g., 99.5% success, p95 < 1.5s, hallucination rate < X%) that gate releases and trigger rollback when exhausted.
• Canary vs blue–green: Canary gradually shifts a small percentage of traffic to a new version with metric guards; blue–green swaps entire environments for fast rollback and minimal downtime.
• Runbooks and rollback: Documented, automated procedures to diagnose issues and revert safely; ensure backward compatibility for prompts/schemas and idempotent deployments.

• A PRR confirms SLOs, capacity, security, observability, and DR are in place before go-live.
• Prefer progressive delivery (canary, feature flags) with automated rollback and clear metric guards.
• AI-specific checks include quality gates, prompt/model versioning, data lineage, and cost guardrails.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now conduct a production readiness review and plan safe, observable releases for model-serving systems.
